lesson.title: Undoing the Sine: The Arcsin Integral Pattern
lesson.summary: The integral of 1/√(1-x²) is arcsin(x) + C, and the same shape with a constant a handles a whole family of square root integrals.
lesson.body:
The arcsin integral is the cleanest of the three inverse trig integrals because you can derive it from a single known fact: d/dx[arcsin(x)] = 1/√(1-x²). Reading that derivative rule backward gives the integral rule immediately: the integral of 1/√(1-x²) dx is arcsin(x) + C. There is no substitution trick required to discover this, it falls straight out of the inverse trig integrals framework from the previous chapter, applied to the one derivative you already had memorized.

The more useful version in practice replaces the 1 under the square root with a general positive constant a²: the integral of 1/√(a²-x²) dx is arcsin(x/a) + C, valid for -a < x < a. You can check this yourself with the chain rule: differentiating arcsin(x/a) gives (1/a) times 1/√(1-(x/a)²), and simplifying the expression under the square root, since 1 - x²/a² equals (a²-x²)/a², turns that into 1/√(a²-x²), matching the integrand exactly. Recognizing when to use this form comes down to spotting a square root of a positive number minus x squared sitting in a denominator.

Try it with a = 2. Evaluate the integral of 1/√(4-x²) dx from x = 0 to x = 1. Here a² = 4 so a = 2, and the antiderivative is arcsin(x/2) + C. By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the definite integral equals arcsin(1/2) minus arcsin(0/2), which is arcsin(1/2) minus arcsin(0), which is π/6 minus 0, or π/6, about 0.5236. Notice this matches the value from the introductory chapter. That is not a coincidence, it happens because x/a equals 1/2 in both computations, so both reduce to evaluating arcsin(1/2).

Now try a fully independent example to build the pattern further. Evaluate the integral of 1/√(1-x²) dx from x = 0 to x = √3/2. The antiderivative is arcsin(x), so the value is arcsin(√3/2) minus arcsin(0). Since sin(60 degrees) equals sin(π/3), which equals √3/2, arcsin(√3/2) = π/3. So the definite integral equals π/3 minus 0, or π/3, about 1.0472. This is much larger than the previous example's π/6 because √3/2 is about 0.866, closer to 1 than 1/2 is, and the function 1/√(1-x²) grows without bound as x approaches 1, so pushing the upper bound closer to 1 sweeps in significantly more area.

This whole pattern is really just the indefinite integral idea, an antiderivative plus an arbitrary constant, applied to one specific derivative you already know cold: the derivative of arcsin. Whenever you see a square root of a difference of squares sitting in a denominator, you are seeing the arcsin derivative running in reverse.
